title: OECD labour markets remain resilient in aggregate while regional job gaps, slowing real-wage recovery, weak mobility, and employment-control practices divide opportunity
source_unit: OECD Employment Outlook 2026: Geographic Disparities in Jobs and Incomes
geography: OECD member countries, national and small-region labour markets, wages, income mobility, skills, and employment regulation

denominator.unit: OECD countries and labour-market indicators covered by the Outlook's aggregate context

employment_rate.unit: percent average OECD employment rate in Q1 2026

participation_rate.unit: percent average OECD labour-force participation rate in Q1 2026

unemployment_rate.unit: percent average OECD unemployment rate in May 2026

weakening.value: Employment and participation remain historically high, but unemployment is rising slightly, employment growth is flattening, and labour-market tightness is easing

observations.method: OECD cross-country labour-market surveillance using national labour-force, wage, employment, and regional data.
observations.uncertainty: Aggregate rates conceal sector, age, gender, migrant, regional, and contract differences; short-term movements are affected by economic, energy, trade, and geopolitical conditions.
observations.subgroup: Workers, jobseekers, young entrants, employers, regional labour markets, migrants, and people with different skills or employment arrangements.
observations.counterinterpretation: High employment and participation can indicate broad resilience, and easing tightness may improve matching or reduce recruitment pressure even if it weakens bargaining power for some workers.

observations.period: Q1 2026; real wages and purchasing room

denominator.unit: OECD countries with comparable real-wage data in Q1 2026

real_wage_growth.unit: percent average annual real-wage growth in Q1 2026, compared with 2.7% in Q1 2025

below_preinflation_wages.unit: OECD countries where real wages remained below Q1 2021 levels

wage_slowdown.value: Real-wage growth in Q1 2026 was lower than a year earlier in two-thirds of the countries analysed

room_mechanism.value: Employment resilience does not guarantee recovery of household purchasing room when wages lag prices and energy or geopolitical shocks add pressure

observations.method: OECD comparison of real wages, inflation-adjusted earnings, wage recovery, and minimum-wage developments.
observations.uncertainty: Real-wage comparisons depend on deflators, reference periods, composition, and country-specific price baskets; they do not measure disposable income, household debt, or living costs directly.
observations.subgroup: Employees, low-paid workers, new hires, households exposed to energy and food costs, employers, and workers with different bargaining coverage.
observations.counterinterpretation: Positive real-wage growth can still improve conditions even when recovery is incomplete, and minimum-wage increases may protect the lowest paid while creating adjustment pressures for some employers.

denominator.unit: OECD small-region employment and income comparison

regional_gap.unit: percentage points or more difference in employment rates across small regions in over half of OECD countries

mobility_constraint.value: Few people move from low- to high-employment regions, and those who move are often the most employable

capital_region_advantage.value: Capital regions generally offer better employment prospects, reflecting unequal distribution of economic opportunity across places

place_route.value: Where people live shapes jobs, incomes, mobility options, and chances of moving up the income ladder

observations.method: OECD analysis of small-region employment, income, labour mobility, and regional opportunity indicators.
observations.uncertainty: Regional averages do not identify each person's mobility constraints, housing costs, family obligations, discrimination, transport access, or the causal effect of moving.
observations.subgroup: Workers in lagging regions, young people, families, commuters, migrants, high- and low-employability movers, and regional employers or public authorities.
observations.counterinterpretation: People may rationally remain in lower-employment regions because of family, housing, cultural, or quality-of-life ties; local job creation can be more equitable than requiring mobility.

observations.period: 2026; job mobility, bargaining, and employment controls

denominator.unit: OECD employment-regulation and firm labour-market framework

noncompete_prevalence.unit: percent of employees estimated to be bound by non-compete clauses

noncompete_effect.value: Non-compete clauses can reduce job mobility, weaken bargaining power, depress wages, and slow productivity or knowledge diffusion

skills_return.value: Skills and training pay off, but returns depend on occupation, work practices, local opportunity, and training design

policy_route.value: Tailored employment protection, local skills policy, and regional interventions are presented as ways to navigate structural and short-term change

observations.method: OECD analysis of employment regulation, non-compete clauses, job mobility, skills returns, employment protection, and regional labour-market policy.
observations.uncertainty: Reported prevalence and effects vary by country, occupation, contract, enforcement, and study design; the publication does not imply every non-compete has the same effect.
observations.subgroup: Employees, contractors, jobseekers, firms, skilled workers, low-wage workers, innovators, and regulators.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some post-employment restrictions can protect legitimate confidential information or investment, and tailored enforcement may be preferable to blanket prohibition.

related_sources.claim: Complementary OECD sector evidence on tourism workforce, affordability, and regional capacity.
Complementary global employment, informality, youth, and social-protection context.

boundary: This record adds an OECD labour-market and regional-opportunity lens on employment resilience, real wages, geographic gaps, mobility, skills, non-competes, and bargaining power. It uses aggregate cross-country and regional evidence, not individual job histories, causal wage estimates for every worker, household budgets, or proof that AI caused current youth or regional outcomes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official OECD Employment Outlook 2026 publication pages reviewed for aggregate labour-market rates, real-wage recovery, regional employment gaps, labour mobility, non-compete prevalence, skills returns, and employment-protection policy.
